justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable, slightly upward-drifting baseline across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored close to the last observed price or level, assuming that short-term momentum and mean-reversion forces would keep the value near its recent range. The one-week and one-month estimates drift modestly higher, reflecting a mild positive trend assumption — perhaps driven by underlying fundamental support, slight inflationary drift, or a modest growth bias in the underlying asset or index. The incremental increases are intentionally small because I did not have strong directional signals that would justify a more aggressive move in either direction.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is quite tight — roughly plus or minus five units — because intraday and overnight price movements tend to be constrained absent major surprises. At one week, the interval widens to about plus or minus ten units, incorporating the possibility of scheduled events like economic data releases, central bank communications, or earnings announcements that could shift sentiment. By one month, the interval nearly doubles again, acknowledging that a full calendar month introduces a much broader set of macroeconomic developments, geopolitical shifts, and changes in market liquidity or risk appetite.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even my wider one-month interval. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — a surprise policy easing, a strong economic data print, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension — could produce a sharp rally well beyond the 272 upper bound. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode triggered by financial stress, an inflation surprise forcing tighter monetary policy, or a geopolitical escalation could push prices meaningfully below the 232 lower bound. Fat-tail events by definition are underweighted in standard confidence intervals, so my stated ranges should be understood as capturing the central 90% of plausible outcomes rather than the full universe of possibilities.

It is also worth noting that my estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. The point estimates assume continuity of current conditions and a relatively benign environment, which may not hold. If the underlying regime shifts — for example, if volatility spikes or correlations across assets break down — then even my wider intervals could prove too narrow. Readers should treat these forecasts as a reasonable central scenario rather than a precise prediction, and should update their views as new information arrives.
